study_type.claude: Repository mining (longitudinal git/ticketing data mining with Bayesian hierarchical modeling)

research_method.claude: Quantitative longitudinal mining of git and ticketing data; Bayesian hierarchical Weibull models (brms/Stan) with within- vs between-person disaggregation; counterfactual simulations
research_method.nlm: Quantitative repository mining; longitudinal Bayesian hierarchical modeling with Weibull distributions separating within-person, between-person and organizational variation
research_method.value: Longitudinal mining of git and ticketing data collected by a software-metrics tool; Bayesian hierarchical Weibull models (brms/Stan) of monthly median cycle time with random effects for organization and user and within- vs between-person disaggregation of predictors (coding days, merged PRs, defect tickets, degree centrality, comments per PR); 55,619 user-month observations
research_method.note: Counterfactual simulations reported only by Claude (not contradicted).

context.claude: Industry; organizations of varied sizes and industries (Technology, Finance, Government, Insurance, Retail, others) using Pluralsight Flow; 11,398 users in 216 organizations
context.nlm: Industry; 216 commercial organizations across Technology, Finance, Government, Insurance, Retail and other sectors; 11,398 contributors
context.value: industry; 216 organizations of varied sizes and sectors (Technology, Finance, Government, Insurance, Retail, others) using a software-metrics tool (Pluralsight Flow, now Flow at Appfire); 11,398 developers, 55,619 user-month observations
context.note: Non-random sample of organizations that adopted the tool; authors were Pluralsight employees.

dora_applied.note: Referenced only: cycle time positioned as conceptually close to DORA lead time.

space_applied.note: Referenced only (Claude: via practitioner critiques; NotebookLM: productivity frameworks discussion).

ai_discussed.note: No AI in data or analysis; AI only in related literature.

remote_covid.note: Work mode not reported by either; no remote/COVID terms in the full text.

data_window.value: 12 months in 2022 (ticket closure observed until March 7, 2023)
data_window.note: Cutoff date reported only by Claude (not contradicted).

cat_productivity.note: Borderline: cycle time (ticket creation to completion, i.e., task completion time) framed as a distal productivity/velocity indicator; Claude labels it Productivity/Delivery, NotebookLM Delivery/Speed.

cat_quality.note: Percent defect tickets (unplanned bug work) as predictor.

cat_collaboration.note: Degree centrality in the PR collaboration network and comments per PR.

cat_satisfaction.note: Well-being/surveillance concerns only discussed as risks of metric use; no satisfaction measure.

cat_activity.note: Coding days per week (days with at least one commit) and total merged PRs.

cat_delivery.note: Cycle time is the dependent variable.

cat_devex.note: DevEx only referenced (NotebookLM); Developer Thriving referenced (Claude).

cat_agile.note: Within-quarter month is a business-calendar effect, not an agile/process metric.

cat_survey.note: No survey data analysed; self-report only recommended for future measurement.

evidence.quote: This dataset includes 55,619 observations across 12 months in 2022 from 11,398 users in 216 organizations of varying sizes and industries.
Through Bayesian hierarchical modeling that appropriately separates individual and organizational variation, we examine how coding time, task scoping, and collaboration patterns affect cycle time
Specifically, we modeled cycle time as distributed Weibull with two parameters, λ (scale), and k (shape).
professional software developer users from these organizations described their main industries as ranging from Technology, Finance, Government, Insurance, Retail, and others
Formerly Pluralsight Flow, now Flow at Appfire.

We analyze cycle time—a widely-used metric measuring time from ticket creation to completion—using a dataset of over 55,000 observations across 216 organizations.

Because lower cycle times are thought to indicate faster delivery times and more efficient software processes, cycle time has long been taken as a key indicator of team health, developer productivity, and team efficiency
Coding days was summarized as the average number of days per week that a developer made at least one commit.
To calculate this, we counted the number of merged pull requests for each user for each month.
To account for this possibility, for each user, for each month, we computed the percent of tickets that were defect tickets.
We measured collaboration by calculating degree centrality.
Another indicator of collaboration is the frequency of comments within PRs.
